videos.script: Does a longer trip mean a longer delivery? Of course it does. But by how much, and how reliably? {{question}} Put distance across the bottom and minutes up the side. Then draw one dot for each of the four hundred deliveries. {{dots}} The dots form a cloud, and the cloud rises from left to right. That rise is the answer to the first question. {{rise}} How tight the cloud is answers the second. Here it is fairly tight, but no delivery sits exactly where the distance alone would put it. {{tight}} A straight line through the cloud summarises it. About two minutes more for every kilometre. {{line}} And then the line tempts you. Follow it past the last dot, out to sixty kilometres, and it predicts a hundred and fifty minutes. Nothing measured that. {{tempt}} This lesson is about the scatterplot. What to do when the dots pile up, how to add a third variable as bubbles, when a line helps, and when it starts to lie. {{plan}}
